topics.title: C# Fundamentals
topics.summary: Core C# syntax, value vs reference types, and the .NET type system.
keyPoints: Value types (struct, int, bool) on the stack vs reference types (class) on the heap
Nullable reference types and the null-forgiving/null-conditional operators (?., ??)
var vs explicit typing, and static typing enforced at compile time
Properties (get/set) as syntactic sugar over backing fields

interviewQA.question: What's the difference between a value type and a reference type in C#, and where is each stored?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Value types (structs, primitives like int/bool) hold their data directly, and copying them copies the data itself — they're typically allocated on the stack when local, though boxed value types live on the heap. Reference types (classes) hold a pointer to data on the heap, so copying a reference type variable copies the reference, not the underlying object, meaning both variables point to the same instance. This affects behavior significantly: mutating a struct passed by value doesn't affect the caller's copy, while mutating a class instance does.
interviewQA.tip: Give a quick code example showing a struct copy vs a class reference sharing state.

topics.title: OOP in C#
topics.summary: Classes, interfaces, and inheritance as implemented in C#, including access modifiers.
keyPoints: Access modifiers: public, private, protected, internal
Interfaces vs abstract classes; C# allows multiple interface implementation
Sealed classes/methods to prevent further inheritance/overriding
Polymorphism via virtual/override keywords

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between 'override' and 'new' when hiding a base class method in C#?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: 'override' requires the base method to be marked virtual (or abstract) and provides true runtime polymorphism — calling the method through a base class reference still invokes the derived class's implementation. 'new' hides the base method entirely rather than overriding it; which version runs depends on the compile-time type of the reference, not the actual runtime object, so calling it through a base reference calls the base version even if the object is actually a derived instance. This distinction trips up many developers and is a common interview gotcha.
interviewQA.tip: Emphasize that 'new' is resolved at compile time based on the reference type — that's the key gotcha.

topics.title: Collections & LINQ Basics
topics.summary: Generic collections and LINQ, C#'s query syntax for filtering and transforming data.
keyPoints: Generic collections: List<T>, Dictionary<K,V>, HashSet<T>
LINQ query syntax vs method (fluent) syntax
Deferred execution: LINQ queries don't run until enumerated
Common operators: Where, Select, OrderBy, GroupBy, FirstOrDefault

interviewQA.question: What does 'deferred execution' mean in LINQ, and why does it sometimes cause bugs?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: A LINQ query built with methods like Where or Select doesn't actually execute when it's defined — it builds an expression tree/enumerator that only runs when you iterate it (via foreach, ToList, Count, etc.). This means if the underlying data source changes between defining the query and enumerating it, or if a captured variable in a closure changes, the results can differ from what you expected at definition time. Calling .ToList() or .ToArray() forces immediate execution and 'freezes' the result if that's the behavior you want.
interviewQA.tip: Give an example: a loop variable captured in a Select() closure before ToList() is called.

topics.title: Exception Handling
topics.summary: C#'s structured exception handling and best practices for robust error handling.
keyPoints: try/catch/finally, and catching specific exception types (most specific first)
Custom exceptions by inheriting from Exception
using statement / IDisposable for deterministic resource cleanup
Avoid catching general Exception silently — rethrow with 'throw;' to preserve stack trace

interviewQA.question: What's the difference between 'throw;' and 'throw ex;' when rethrowing an exception in a catch block?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: 'throw;' rethrows the current exception while preserving its original stack trace, so the exception still shows where it was first thrown. 'throw ex;' resets the stack trace to the current catch block's location, losing the original throw point, which makes debugging much harder because you lose the real origin of the failure. As a rule, always use bare 'throw;' when rethrowing the same exception object.
interviewQA.tip: This is a classic gotcha question — make the stack trace difference explicit.

topics.title: Delegates, Events & Lambda Expressions
topics.summary: The foundation of callbacks and event-driven code in C#, and how lambdas make them concise.
keyPoints: A delegate is a type-safe function pointer: Func<T,TResult>, Action<T>, Predicate<T>
Events are a controlled wrapper over delegates, restricting outside code to subscribe/unsubscribe only
Lambda expressions (x => x * 2) are shorthand for anonymous delegate implementations
Multicast delegates let one event notify multiple subscribers

interviewQA.question: What's the difference between a delegate and an event in C#?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: A delegate is a general-purpose type-safe function reference that external code can freely invoke or reassign. An event is built on top of a delegate but restricts outside code to only += (subscribe) or -= (unsubscribe) — only the declaring class can actually invoke it — which enforces proper publisher/subscriber encapsulation.
interviewQA.tip: Give a concrete example: a Button.Click event that any code can subscribe to, but only the Button class can raise.

topics.title: LINQ Advanced Queries
topics.summary: Writing expressive, composable data queries directly in C# instead of manual loops.
keyPoints: Method syntax (.Where().Select()) vs query syntax (from x in ... select ...) — functionally equivalent
Deferred execution: a LINQ query doesn't run until enumerated (foreach, .ToList())
GroupBy, Join, OrderBy for relational-style operations over in-memory or IQueryable data
IEnumerable (in-memory) vs IQueryable (translated to SQL for Entity Framework) — know which you're using

interviewQA.question: What does 'deferred execution' mean in LINQ, and why can it cause a subtle bug?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: A LINQ query built with method syntax isn't actually executed when defined — it's a description of the query that only runs when enumerated (foreach, ToList, etc.). The subtle bug: if the underlying data changes between defining the query and enumerating it, or if you enumerate it twice, you may get different or unexpectedly re-computed results each time.
interviewQA.tip: Mention .ToList() as the fix to force immediate, one-time evaluation and 'freeze' the results.

topics.title: ASP.NET Core MVC & Web API
topics.summary: Building web applications and REST APIs on ASP.NET Core, and its request pipeline.
keyPoints: Middleware pipeline: request flows through ordered middleware (auth, routing, exception handling)
Controllers, action methods, model binding, and attribute routing
Dependency injection is built into the framework via IServiceCollection
Filters (Authorization, Action, Exception filters) for cross-cutting logic

interviewQA.question: Explain the ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline and why the order of middleware registration matters.
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Each middleware component in ASP.NET Core is a function that can process a request, then call the next middleware in the chain (or short-circuit it), forming a pipeline configured in Program.cs/Startup.cs with app.Use... calls. Order matters because each middleware wraps the ones after it — for example, UseAuthentication must run before UseAuthorization, and exception-handling middleware should be registered early so it can catch errors from everything downstream. Registering middleware in the wrong order can silently break auth checks or leave errors unhandled.
interviewQA.tip: Give the classic example: UseAuthentication before UseAuthorization, exception handler first.

topics.title: Entity Framework Core
topics.summary: Microsoft's ORM for .NET, covering the DbContext, change tracking, and migrations.
keyPoints: DbContext as the unit-of-work/session, DbSet<T> per entity
Change tracking: EF detects modified entities and generates the right SQL on SaveChanges
Migrations: code-first schema evolution (Add-Migration, Update-Database)
Eager (Include), lazy, and explicit loading of related data — and the N+1 query trap

interviewQA.question: What is the N+1 query problem in Entity Framework, and how do you avoid it?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: The N+1 problem happens when you fetch a list of N entities, then access a related navigation property on each one separately — with lazy loading enabled, this triggers one additional query per entity (N extra queries) instead of one combined query, badly hurting performance as N grows. The fix is eager loading: use .Include() (and .ThenInclude() for nested relations) in the original query so EF Core generates a single query with the necessary joins upfront. Tools like MiniProfiler or EF's logging can help spot N+1 patterns in real apps.
interviewQA.tip: Mention .Include()/.ThenInclude() by name — interviewers look for that specific API knowledge.

topics.title: Dependency Injection in .NET
topics.summary: The built-in DI container in ASP.NET Core and how service lifetimes affect application behavior.
keyPoints: Service lifetimes: Transient (new every time), Scoped (per request), Singleton (app lifetime)
Registering services via IServiceCollection (AddTransient/AddScoped/AddSingleton)
Constructor injection as the standard pattern
Common bug: injecting a Scoped service into a Singleton (captive dependency)

interviewQA.question: What's a 'captive dependency' in .NET DI, and how does it happen?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: A captive dependency occurs when a longer-lived service (like a Singleton) holds a reference to a shorter-lived service (like a Scoped DbContext), which gets injected once at the Singleton's creation and then 'captured' for the app's entire lifetime instead of being properly scoped per request. This can cause stale data, threading issues (DbContext isn't thread-safe), or memory growth. The fix is to inject IServiceScopeFactory or IServiceProvider into the Singleton and manually create a scope when you need the Scoped service, rather than injecting it directly.
interviewQA.tip: DbContext-in-a-Singleton is the classic real-world example to cite.

topics.title: Async/Await Programming
topics.summary: C#'s asynchronous programming model for scalable I/O-bound applications.
keyPoints: async/await compiles to a state machine, not a new thread by default
Task vs Task<T>, and ConfigureAwait(false) to avoid context-capture deadlocks in libraries
async all the way: avoid mixing .Result/.Wait() with async code (deadlock risk)
Task.WhenAll for running independent async operations concurrently

interviewQA.question: Why can calling .Result on a Task cause a deadlock in an ASP.NET application, and how do you avoid it?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: In contexts with a SynchronizationContext (like older ASP.NET or UI apps), 'await' by default captures the current context and resumes on it after the awaited task completes. If you block synchronously with .Result or .Wait() on that same context's thread, the thread is stuck waiting for the async method to finish, but the async method can't resume because it needs that same blocked thread/context — a deadlock. The fix is to use async all the way up the call stack (await instead of blocking), and library code should use ConfigureAwait(false) to avoid capturing the context when it doesn't need to resume on it.
interviewQA.tip: This is a very common senior-level .NET interview question — know it cold.

topics.title: Unit Testing with xUnit/NUnit
topics.summary: Writing fast, isolated tests for .NET code and mocking dependencies with a framework like Moq.
keyPoints: xUnit: [Fact] for a single test, [Theory] + [InlineData] for parametrized tests
Arrange-Act-Assert structure keeps tests readable and consistent
Moq: new Mock<IRepo>(), .Setup(x => x.Get(1)).Returns(...), .Verify() for interaction checks
Dependency injection makes classes testable by letting you substitute real dependencies with mocks

interviewQA.question: Why does constructor-based dependency injection make a class easier to unit test?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: When dependencies are passed into the constructor (as interfaces) rather than created internally with 'new', a test can pass in a mock implementation instead of the real one — letting you isolate the class under test from databases, APIs, or other side effects entirely.
interviewQA.tip: Mention that a class that 'new's up its own dependencies internally is a common testability anti-pattern.

topics.title: SignalR & Real-Time Communication
topics.summary: Pushing live updates from server to client without the client having to poll.
keyPoints: SignalR abstracts over WebSockets, falling back to Server-Sent Events or long polling if needed
Hubs are server-side classes clients connect to and invoke methods on
Groups let you broadcast to a subset of connected clients (e.g. users in one chat room)
Scaling SignalR across multiple server instances requires a backplane (e.g. Redis) to sync connections

interviewQA.question: Why does SignalR need a backplane like Redis when you scale to multiple server instances?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Each server instance only knows about the WebSocket connections it's directly holding. If a message needs to reach a client connected to a different instance, that instance has no way to know about it — a backplane like Redis pub/sub relays messages across all instances so any server can broadcast to any connected client, regardless of which instance it's on.
interviewQA.tip: Mention sticky sessions as a related but insufficient partial solution on its own.

topics.title: Microservices with .NET
topics.summary: Building distributed .NET systems with independent, deployable services.
keyPoints: gRPC and REST for inter-service communication; message brokers (RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus) for async
API Gateway pattern (e.g., Ocelot, YARP) to unify entry points
Health checks and resilience with Polly (retry, circuit breaker, timeout policies)
Containerizing .NET services with Docker for consistent deployment

interviewQA.question: How would you add resilience (retries, circuit breaking) to HTTP calls between .NET microservices?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Use the Polly library integrated via IHttpClientFactory's AddPolicyHandler, defining policies like exponential backoff retries for transient failures and a circuit breaker that stops sending requests to a failing downstream service for a cooldown period once a failure threshold is hit. This prevents cascading failures — instead of every request timing out slowly against a dead service, the circuit 'opens' and fails fast, giving the downstream service room to recover. Combine this with sensible timeouts so a single slow dependency can't exhaust thread pool resources.
interviewQA.tip: Mention IHttpClientFactory + Polly together — that's the standard modern .NET pattern.

topics.title: Design Patterns in C#
topics.summary: Applying classic design patterns idiomatically within .NET's type system and conventions.
keyPoints: Repository & Unit of Work patterns over EF Core (with caveats — EF's DbContext already implements both)
Factory and Builder patterns for complex object construction
Decorator pattern via .NET's DI 'decoration' support or manual wrapping
CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) with libraries like MediatR

interviewQA.question: Is wrapping Entity Framework Core's DbContext in a Repository pattern actually a good idea? Why or why not?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: It's a genuinely debated practice: DbContext already implements the Unit of Work pattern and DbSet<T> already behaves like a repository (queryable, trackable), so an additional Repository layer can be redundant and sometimes leaks EF-specific concerns (like IQueryable) through a supposedly abstract interface anyway. It can still be justified for genuinely swapping data sources, simplifying unit testing without a real database, or centralizing complex query logic — but many experienced .NET teams now favor using EF Core directly in a thin service layer instead of a generic repository wrapper, especially for CQRS-style read queries.
interviewQA.tip: A balanced answer ('it depends, here's when it helps vs hurts') is stronger than a flat yes/no.

topics.title: Performance & Memory Management
topics.summary: How the .NET garbage collector works and how to write allocation-conscious, high-performance C#.
keyPoints: Generational GC: Gen 0/1/2, and why short-lived object allocation is cheap
IDisposable and the 'using' pattern for deterministic cleanup of unmanaged resources
Span<T> and Memory<T> for allocation-free slicing of arrays/strings
Server vs Workstation GC modes for throughput vs latency trade-offs

interviewQA.question: Why would you use Span<T> instead of an array slice or substring in performance-critical C# code?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Span<T> represents a contiguous, type-safe view over existing memory (array, stack, or unmanaged memory) without copying it, whereas operations like array.Skip().Take() or string.Substring() allocate a brand-new array or string on the heap. In hot paths processing large amounts of data (parsers, serializers), avoiding those allocations significantly reduces GC pressure and improves throughput. The trade-off is that Span<T> is a ref struct, so it can't be stored on the heap, used in async methods directly, or boxed, which constrains where it can be used.
interviewQA.tip: Mention the ref struct constraint — it's a common follow-up question.

topics.title: Azure Cloud Integration
topics.summary: Deploying and integrating .NET applications with common Azure PaaS services.
keyPoints: Azure App Service for hosting, with deployment slots for zero-downtime releases
Azure Functions for serverless, event-driven .NET code
Azure SQL / Cosmos DB integration and managed identities for secretless auth
Application Insights for telemetry, logging, and distributed tracing

interviewQA.question: How would you achieve a zero-downtime deployment for an ASP.NET Core app on Azure App Service?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Use deployment slots: deploy the new version to a staging slot separate from production, let it warm up and run smoke tests against it, then perform a slot swap, which Azure does by re-routing traffic instantly (and swapping app settings if configured) rather than restarting the production instance. Because the new version was already running and warmed up in staging before the swap, there's no cold-start delay visible to users, and if something's wrong, you can swap back immediately for a fast rollback.
interviewQA.tip: Mention the ability to instantly swap back as a rollback strategy — interviewers like operational thinking.

topics.title: gRPC in .NET
topics.summary: A high-performance RPC framework for service-to-service communication, common in microservices.
keyPoints: Uses Protocol Buffers (protobuf) for a compact binary format and strongly-typed contracts
Built on HTTP/2, enabling multiplexed streaming (unary, server-streaming, client-streaming, bidirectional)
The .proto file is the single source of truth, generating client/server code for multiple languages
Generally faster and smaller-payload than JSON/REST, but less human-readable/debuggable

interviewQA.question: When would you choose gRPC over a REST API for a new internal service?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: gRPC is a strong fit for internal, high-throughput service-to-service communication where performance and strict typed contracts matter — its binary protobuf payloads are smaller and faster to (de)serialize than JSON, and it supports true bidirectional streaming that REST doesn't handle naturally. REST/JSON remains better for public APIs needing broad, easy client compatibility and human-readable debugging.
interviewQA.tip: Mention that gRPC's HTTP/2 requirement can complicate some browser/proxy setups without a gateway.

topics.title: .NET Performance Profiling & Diagnostics
topics.summary: Finding real bottlenecks in a running .NET application using built-in and third-party tooling.
keyPoints: dotnet-trace, dotnet-counters, and dotnet-dump are built-in CLI diagnostic tools
The Server GC mode is better for throughput on multi-core servers than Workstation GC
Common bottlenecks: excessive allocations, sync-over-async deadlocks, N+1 EF Core queries
Application Insights/APM tools correlate performance data with real production traffic

interviewQA.question: What's a 'sync-over-async' deadlock in ASP.NET, and how do you avoid it?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: It happens when synchronous code blocks on an async call (e.g. calling .Result or .Wait() on a Task) inside a context that captures the synchronization context, like classic ASP.NET — the blocking call waits for the continuation, but the continuation is waiting for the thread the blocking call is holding, causing a deadlock. Avoid it by using async all the way up the call stack instead of mixing sync and async.
interviewQA.tip: Mention ConfigureAwait(false) as a partial historical mitigation, though 'async all the way' is the real fix.
